beats.say: Two assistants pass ninety percent of the same test. Would you expect them to make the same mistakes? Open the score into its individual questions. One assistant struggles with a small, important group that the other usually handles. The average has compressed away the difference we need to see.

A benchmark combines tasks with a scoring procedure. Its result describes performance on those tasks under that procedure. We will build a small evaluation, test the checker, inspect hidden failure patterns, and follow the evidence needed to compare systems fairly.

All the examples here are small teaching fixtures. Keep the question identities in view as their scores are grouped, sampled, and moved between datasets. That lets us see exactly what each reported number measures.

Imagine changing the model inside a library assistant. Both candidates should receive the same questions, available evidence, response requirements, and scoring rules. Record the prompt, tools, sampling settings, and attempt budget as well. Each model still needs its own correct chat formatting.

Now give the second system five retrieved passages where the first received three. Its answers may improve, and that is useful to measure. The experiment now compares two complete systems. Retrieval changed along with the model, so the report must describe both changes.

Public benchmarks also have distinct contracts. Multiple-choice knowledge, executable programs, and human preferences score different units. Use those results to choose promising candidates, then compare them on the task your application actually needs.

Before trusting those library scores, inspect what each test asks. The article’s executable companion uses three fictional platform policies: freeze deployment needs commander approval, a threshold breach calls the rollback runbook, and exposed tokens need revocation within fifteen minutes. Preserve the question, authoritative evidence, required facts and forbidden claims together. These are supplied teaching policies, not general deployment instructions.

Give each row a unique identity. Duplicating an identity can overwrite or ambiguously join the result. Then compare each gold requirement with its cited evidence before scoring an answer. A required claim absent from that source can punish a grounded answer or reward invented permission. The actual validator checks unique IDs and literal required phrases; it does not establish the source’s authority or semantic truth.

Now deliberately require keep deploying from the rollback source. That requirement has no support, so repair the gold row first. Preserve a reviewed expected answer and label the failure severity. A useful golden set mirrors the service’s requests, including critical slices and valid abstentions. Testing the model against an impossible answer key would measure the key’s defect.

Our library rule says that borrowed books are due on Friday. A cheap checker looks for the words books and Friday. The first answer repeats the rule correctly. Both the phrase check and our reviewed semantic label agree that it preserves the deadline.

Replace the answer with books are due after Friday. The same two words remain, so the literal checker still passes it. Our reviewed label rejects the changed deadline. This probe exposes a specific false positive in the checker.

A familiar abbreviation can fail in the other direction. Return the books by Friday preserves this rule. The displayed answer shortens the weekday to Fri, so our exact word check misses it. Keep exact checks for exact fields, and validate meaning with reviewed examples that include these harder cases.

Follow the commander-approval fact through the actual request. First inspect the final context sent to the model, after permissions, ranking and token-budget selection. If that clause is absent there, the response never received the required evidence. A relevant document retrieved earlier but dropped during assembly does not count as evidence the model saw.

Keep the context complete and change only the answer: it mentions the freeze but substitutes an on-call engineer for commander approval. Now the first observed failure is generation or instruction following. The article’s literal classifier reports bad retrieval, bad generation or pass by checking required phrases in that order. It inherits the same negation and paraphrase limits as its checker.

An exact citation can identify a source while an attached claim contradicts it. Exercise correct answer with correct page, correct answer with wrong page, and a negated answer with correct page. Source identity and semantic entailment are separate checks. Preserve context, answer and source versions so a repair targets the observed boundary and then repeats the complete regression path.

Retrieval precision and recall answer different questions. In a supplied ranked list with relevance flags one, zero, one, precision at the first relevant rank is one, and at the third is two thirds. Averaging those precisions gives five sixths, about point eight three three. This rank-weighted precision rewards useful context appearing early; it cannot discover a required fact missing from every returned chunk.

For reference-based context recall, divide covered reference facts by required reference facts. Suppose the context contains two of three required facts. Recall is two thirds. If the response states only those two supported facts, its faithfulness is two supported claims divided by two claims, or one. The response is still incomplete. A supported claim can also repeat an outdated source.

Current Ragas response relevancy generates questions from the response and compares their embeddings with the original question, averaging cosine similarities. It measures topical alignment, not truth. Keep retrieval coverage, supported claims, completeness and relevance separate, and check model-based scoring against reviewed labels. These examples calculate the metric formulas directly. They do not demonstrate a Ragas model or embedding evaluation.

Public benchmarks help shortlist capabilities. MMLU covers fifty-seven subjects with four choices per question. Uniform guessing has expected accuracy one fourth, not a minimum any finite run must achieve. Common evaluations use five demonstrations and choice-token probabilities; generated-answer parsing is another protocol. Changing that path changes what a score measures, even when both results are percentages.

MMLU-Pro adds reviewed, reasoning-focused questions with up to ten choices. Exactly ten choices give a one-tenth guessing expectation. Its reported chain-of-thought advantage belongs to the tested models and protocol. GPQA instead uses expert biology, physics and chemistry: Extended has five hundred forty-six questions, main four hundred forty-eight, and Diamond one hundred ninety-eight. Validator-based filtering changes the subsets, so name the actual split.

The original GPQA study’s non-expert validators scored about thirty-four percent on Extended despite internet access; that historical result is not a universal human ceiling. HELM evaluates several dimensions, including accuracy, calibration, robustness, fairness and bias. Its public scenarios do not measure private policy compliance, but its modular framework accepts custom scenarios. Run the relevant private evaluation instead of treating an unrelated leaderboard as release authority.

GSM8K contains about eight and a half thousand grade-school word problems, typically two to eight arithmetic steps. Its reference solutions mark the final number after four hash characters; a particular harness decides whether model outputs need that delimiter. MATH has twelve thousand five hundred competition problems with worked solutions. Extracted final-answer correctness and a valid derivation are different contracts; record parser and tool access.

Harder suites also need exact versions. Humanity’s Last Exam finalized its original twenty-five-hundred-question public set in April twenty-twenty-five and retains a private holdout. Its site lists Rolling in October twenty-twenty-five and Diamond in September twenty-twenty-six. FrontierMath spans advanced-undergraduate through research-level tiers. Its Tiers One through Four page reports a June twelfth twenty-twenty-six version-two release addressing errors in forty-two percent of problems. Older scores do not transfer automatically.

ARC-AGI-two asks a system to infer a rule from example input and output grids, then apply it to a new grid. Symbolic interpretation, composition and context-dependent rules go beyond geometric rotation. Public, semi-private and private sets have different exposure histories. A supplied toy grid can demonstrate rule application, but it is not a scored ARC task or evidence that a platform assistant preserves deployment permissions.

HumanEval measures function synthesis with one hundred sixty-four handwritten Python problems and unit tests. SWE-bench’s original collection has two thousand two hundred ninety-four issue-based tasks across twelve Python repositories. The system must inspect a repository, edit code and submit a patch. Those are different task contracts, and neither percentage directly measures our library or policy answers.

The SWE-bench Docker harness applies the patch and grades named Fail-to-Pass repair tests and Pass-to-Pass regression tests under its parser rules. Inspect which assertions those selected tests exercise. A patch can pass selected checks while an omitted behavior remains wrong. A resolved label describes that harness result; it is not proof that every repository test or intended behavior was preserved.

The measured coding system includes model, prompt loop, tools, repository environment and attempt budget. Ten agent attempts can contain many model and tool calls. Preserve failures, timeouts, selected tests and the returned patch, then compare at a common budget or report the tradeoff. Changing the agent scaffold can change the result while model weights stay fixed.

Human review improves a suite without guaranteeing flawless tasks. SWE-bench Verified selected five hundred tasks. OpenAI stopped reporting it in February twenty-twenty-six after finding material test or description issues in fifty-nine point four percent of a selected one-hundred-thirty-eight-task subset that o three did not consistently solve. That denominator is the selected subset, not all five hundred tasks.

The same audit found signs that tested frontier models could reproduce human fixes or verbatim task details for some tasks. A public test may therefore mix engineering ability with exposure. OpenAI initially recommended SWE-bench Pro, then retracted that recommendation in July twenty-twenty-six after auditing its seven hundred thirty-one public tasks and estimating that about thirty percent were broken.
